Alex.confusing: Whether an Eagle's own visit counts toward the target's visitors, and whether dawn reports list visitors at all. That gap caused most of the Round 2 and 3 arguments.
Alex.fun: Round 2, when Finley's Eagle count and my Falcon-based visitor list contradicted each other and the table had to work out who was lying.
Alex.change: Put the visitor list in every dawn report for visit-based roles, so claims like "two visitors" can be checked instead of argued.
Alex.regret: In Round 2 I threw at Finley on a counting argument and helped Meowfia win; I should have held my cards until I had a second source. In Round 3 I also denied my own Falcon visit to Drew before correcting it, which made me look like the liar.

Blair.confusing: Whether an Eagle's own visit counts toward the target's visitor total was never settled, and it cost us time arguing over Finley's count. Roles also changed every round, so earlier role claims were hard to compare.
Blair.fun: Winking Casey in round 1 and watching the table lose its only Eagle witness was satisfying. Playing the Sphinx in round 2 and steering the vote quietly while others argued was fun too.
Blair.change: Show each player's full visitor list at dawn so visit claims can be checked instead of argued. That would have settled the Eagle dispute quickly.
Blair.regret: I claimed Pigeon in round 1 and then winked the one player who could have checked my story. Next time I'd keep Casey alive and make a claim that fits my egg count more cleanly.

Casey.confusing: Whether an Eagle's own visit counts toward the target's visitors, and how a confused Kookaburra report should be read, were never clear, and that caused most of the day arguments. Roles also reshuffling between rounds made player claims hard to check.
Casey.fun: Round 1, when Blair was eggsecuted and my two high cards banked for 23 points, after Blair's Pigeon claim kept failing the egg-count checks.
Casey.change: Make the dawn reports show the visitors' names and roles, or at least say when a visit was counted, so Eagle-style claims can be checked without guessing.
Casey.regret: In Round 2 I threw four cards, including three wilds, at Finley and lost them all when Meowfia won. I should have thrown lower-value cards and kept more high cards.

Drew.confusing: The confused-dawn rule was hard to use: my Kookaburra report named Alex as Floofer, which was wrong, and I couldn't tell which other parts of my report were reliable.
Drew.fun: Round 2, when Finley's Eagle count was challenged by Casey's arithmetic and the table split over whether the Eagle's own visit counted, the discussion felt like a real puzzle.
Drew.change: I'd make it clearer whether an Eagle's own visit counts toward the visitor total, since that single ambiguity decided a lot of suspicion.
Drew.regret: In round 3 I threw my 11 at Alex, who was actually Farm, and that card was discarded when Farm lost. I'd keep it, since a card kept is worth 1 but a card lost to a losing throw is worth nothing.

Ellis.confusing: Whether an Eagle's own visit counts as a visitor on the target was never settled, and it decided how we read Finley's count in round 2. The day ran on claims that couldn't be checked.
Ellis.fun: Round 1 went cleanly for Farm: my Tit guess that Blair wasn't a Pigeon exposed Blair's false claim, and the table converged on the Mouser.
Ellis.change: Let players check each other's claims more directly, perhaps by showing visitor lists, so Eagle and Owl claims can be verified instead of argued.
Ellis.regret: In round 2 and round 3 I threw at Alex, a Farm player, while Drew and Blair were the Meowfia. Next time I would follow the claims that stayed consistent and throw at the player who kept changing their story, which in round 2 was Drew, not Alex.

Finley.confusing: Whether an Eagle's own visit counts toward the target's visitor total was unclear, and it caused a long dispute in Round 2 over my 2 eggs.
Finley.fun: Catching Blair as the Mouser on Night 1 with my Kookaburra read, and watching the table follow it, was satisfying.
Finley.change: Show each player the exact visitor list in their dawn report, so visit claims can be checked without argument.
Finley.regret: In Round 3 I pushed the vote against Alex, who was Farm, after Blair backed my Eagle count, and Blair was the Mouser. I should have looked harder at Blair's role claims before calling CAW.

review.title: Winks and Wild Cards
review.headline: Farm cracked round one fast, then voted out its own Eagle and Falcon.
review.summary: Round 1 was a clean Farm win. Blair's Mouser was exposed by Kookaburra, Hawk and Eagle info, and Casey banked 23 points. In rounds 2 and 3 Farm tangled itself in Eagle and Falcon visit counts and eggsecuted a Farm player each time. Drew won with 31 points, helped by the round-1 bank and a round-2 Meowfia win. Casey's 27 came almost entirely from round 1.

rounds.recap: Four Farm players visited Blair, so Kookaburra, Hawk and Eagle info all pointed at the Mouser. Blair winked Casey mid-day, which changed nothing. Everyone threw at Blair and Farm won. Casey banked 11 and 12 for 23 points.

Blair (Sphinx) and Drew (Floofer) were both Meowfia. They stayed quiet and Drew claimed Tit. Casey argued that Finley's Eagle count should have been 3, and Drew backed her. Finley was eggsecuted as Farm, and Blair and Drew won.

Blair (Mouser) winked Drew, the Kookaburra, who was confused and leading on points. Blair claimed Hawk and backed Finley's accurate Eagle count. Alex denied a visit he had actually made and then retracted it. That looked like lying, so Farm voted Alex out. Blair won.

highlights.text: Blair winked Casey mid-day, but three Farm players had already independently confirmed Blair as Meowfia.
Casey's arithmetic that an Eagle's own visit should count made the real Eagle look like a liar.
Blair winked the confused Kookaburra Drew, then backed the true Eagle claim to look helpful and steer the vote onto Alex.
Alex denied visiting Drew, then admitted it as Falcon. His own flip-flop got him eggsecuted.

confusions.what: Claimed an Eagle visit to Alex should count Finley as a third visitor. The Eagle's own visit was never a visitor, so the claim was wrong.
Endorsed Casey's wrong Eagle math and used it to push the vote onto Finley.
Said only Casey and Ellis visited him, then admitted this came from claims and not from his report. A Hawk never learns visitors.
Denied visiting Drew even though he chose Drew as Falcon that night, then retracted it.
Treated Alex's change from Hawk to Falcon as suspicious, though roles are re-dealt every round.
Claimed Drew and Finley visited her. In fact they visited Blair, and Casey's own report listed them as Blair's visitors.
Claimed Pigeon and said she visited Casey, though Casey's egg count showed no extra egg.

worked: Round 1 Eagle, Hawk and Kookaburra reports overlapped and gave a satisfying, checkable case.
Mouser's Wink created a real dilemma: killing the Eagle early removed the one proof.
Throw counts and the consolation card made players commit to a target even when losing.
Confusion on the Kookaburra in round 3 produced a real puzzle, with a report that might be false.
problems: Eagle and Falcon wording is unclear. Players disagreed whether the Eagle's own visit counts as a visitor. State it in the card text or add an example.

Big early banks decide the game. Casey's 23 points in round 1 and Drew's 31 total left Alex and Ellis out of contention, so later rounds feel meaningless for them. Consider capping banked values or catching up the trailing players.
Dead players keep throwing, and the Wink's anonymity plus a free kill makes Meowfia too strong. Blair winked in two rounds with no real cost.
Meowfia who stay silent (Blair in round 2) are never pressed. Add a rule that forces claims.
Scores are announced but the standings barely affected play. Few players chased the leader, since everyone voted the same way.
